title: In return to Toronto, Bo Bichette gets emotional: ‘I gave it everything I had’
content:
TORONTO — Bo Bichette spent seven seasons in Toronto as a stoic staple. He was the unfazed force in the middle of the Blue Jays lineup, rarely affected by the emotional swings around him.

There was an occasional burst of passion. He paused to collect his thoughts while discussing former teammate Marcus Semien after the 2021 season. He lingered in an embrace with former third base coach Luis Rivera, who announced his retirement after Toronto’s 2023 postseason loss. He flicked his bat, swaggering into a jog after a momentous homer in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series.

Those were nothing compared to Monday.

Bichette, returning to Toronto for the first time since signing a three-year $126 million deal with the New York Mets in January, was overcome with emotion. The 28-year-old, staring over cameras and looking out at the turf field, lost his words. His eyes started to fill as he thought about how Toronto fans would welcome him back.

“I gave it everything I had,” Bichette eventually said. “I just hope that’s appreciated.”

It was as if over 700 games worth of memories flooded back in an instant; as if he was reminded of every slapped double down the right field line, every standing ovation and every smirk shared with Vladimir Guerrero Jr., at the same time. The emotion, the infielder said, even surprised himself.

“A lot of things are being brought up at one time right now,” Bichette said.

The former Jays shortstop took multiple moments to collect himself, with bright camera lights directed at his face. It was an opportunity, he said, to reflect on good times. He’s a Met now, one with an opt-out clause after seasons one and two. But the 40,000 Jays fans in attendance and those watching on television remember him for the relentless hits, two All-Star seasons, four postseason runs and one of the best Blue Jay shortstop careers in modern history.

Bichette talked about growing up in baseball with Guerrero, living the best and worst times together. He talked about his decision to leave, understanding his time with the Jays was likely over before he ultimately signed with New York. He talked about returning from a busted knee to play on one leg, as manager John Schneider said, in the World Series.

He talked about his Game 7 homer, one that fell a few outs from being one of the most iconic in Toronto sports history.

That home run is ingrained in his former manager’s mind. Schneider took a mental snapshot, in the chaos of a win-or-die World Series game, of Bichette crossing home plate and meeting the outstretched arms of Guerrero. It’s really the final moment the pair, who played together from the low-minors through last November, shared. Yet, it’s probably their most iconic moment, too.

It’s likely ingrained in the minds of so many Jays fans, as well, anticipating the pinnacle that ultimately eluded Toronto.

“Couldn’t have drawn it up better,” Bichette said. “Obviously, I hoped we would have won.”

Bichette took a few minutes after that home run, he revealed on Monday, ducking into the tunnel by Toronto’s home dugout by himself. He reflected on the swing against Shohei Ohtani he had just crafted. It was, at the time, the ultimate finale for a player that helped define an era for a franchise. He kept that reflection, though, to himself.

That’s what Bichette did for seven seasons in Toronto. He delivered massive hits and lifted the Blue Jays to new heights, while keeping his emotion largely concealed in tunnels, closed clubhouses and to himself. On Monday, though, he was unable to hide it.

Whether or not Bichette wanted it to, the emotion trickled out.
